## Topics covered

-   Least squares (recap of Unit F) and the command `lm`
-   The simple linear regression model
-   Tests and confidence intervals for the slope
-   Confidence and prediction intervals
-   Diagnostic plots: residuals and normal Q-Q plot
-   Multiple linear regression: interpretation of the coefficients

## Back to Unit F

We have already met the [simple linear regression]{.orange} in
[Unit F](un_F.html), with the `forbes` data: we predicted the atmospheric
pressure from the boiling temperature of water. There, we computed:

-   the [least squares]{.blue} estimates $\hat{\alpha}$ and $\hat{\beta}$;
-   the [predicted]{.blue} values, for instance the pressure when water boils at
    $97$ degrees Celsius;
-   the coefficient $R^2$, to measure the goodness of fit.

That analysis was purely [descriptive]{.orange}: it only concerned the $n = 17$
observed locations. In this unit, we make [inference]{.orange}, using the tools of
[Unit I](un_I.html) and [Unit J](un_J.html): standard errors, tests and
confidence intervals.

## Black cherry trees

For $n = 31$ [black cherry trees]{.orange} in the Allegheny National Forest
(Pennsylvania, USA), the data report:

-   the [diameter]{.blue} of the trunk, measured at about $1.37$ m above the
    ground;
-   the [height]{.blue} of the tree;
-   the [volume]{.orange} of timber obtained from the tree, after felling it.

The diameter is easy to measure on a standing tree. The volume, instead, is
known only after the tree has been cut down.

::: callout-note
#### Research question

Can we predict the volume of timber of a tree from its diameter, [before]{.orange}
cutting it down? How precise is the prediction?
:::

## Importing the `trees` data

As done previously, first of all you need to download the file `trees.csv` and
save it on your computer. [Link to the file](data/trees.csv)

```{r}
trees <- read.table("data/trees.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")
```

Alternatively, we can simply obtain them using the link:

```{r}
#| eval: false
path <- "https://tommasorigon.github.io/EnvEcoStat/data/trees.csv"
trees <- read.table(path, header = TRUE, sep = ",")
```

```{r}
str(trees)
```

The variable `Girth` is, despite its name, the diameter of the trunk.

## Preliminary operations

The original measurements are in inches, feet and cubic feet. We convert them
into [centimetres]{.blue}, [metres]{.blue} and [cubic metres]{.blue}, recalling
that $1$ inch $= 2.54$ cm, $1$ foot $= 0.3048$ m and $1$ cubic foot
$= 0.0283$ m$^3$.

```{r}
cherry <- data.frame(
  diameter = round(trees$Girth * 2.54, 1), # cm
  height = round(trees$Height * 0.3048, 1), # m
  volume = round(trees$Volume * 0.0283168, 3) # cubic metres
)
summary(cherry)
```

The height will be used later in this unit.

## The scatterplot

```{r}
plot(cherry$diameter, cherry$volume,
  pch = 16,
  xlab = "Diameter (cm)", ylab = "Volume (cubic metres)"
)
cor(cherry$diameter, cherry$volume)
```

The relationship is strong and approximately [linear]{.orange}.

## The least squares line

In [Unit F](un_F.html), as in the course of Statistics, we denoted the intercept
and the slope by $\alpha$ and $\beta$. From now on, as in the theory lectures,
we denote them by $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$. In a [linear model]{.blue} of the form
$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i$, the [least squares]{.orange} estimates
are equal to $$
\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1\:\bar{x}, \qquad \hat{\beta}_1  = \frac{\text{cov}(x,y)}{\text{var}(x)}.
$$

We use again the functions `my_var` and `my_cov` of [Unit F](un_F.html):

```{r}
my_var <- function(x) mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2
my_cov <- function(x, y) mean(x * y) - mean(x) * mean(y)

x <- cherry$diameter
y <- cherry$volume
beta1_hat <- my_cov(x, y) / my_var(x) # Slope
beta0_hat <- mean(y) - beta1_hat * mean(x) # Intercept
c(beta0_hat, beta1_hat)
```

Each additional centimetre of diameter corresponds, on average, to
$0.056$ m$^3$ of additional timber.

## The command `lm`

In [Unit F](un_F.html) we mentioned that the command `lm` (*linear model*)
computes the same estimates. The [formula]{.blue} `volume ~ diameter` reads
"volume as a function of diameter":

```{r}
fit <- lm(volume ~ diameter, data = cherry)
coef(fit) # Least squares estimates
```

The object `fit` contains much more. For instance, the fitted values
$\hat{\mu}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1x_i$ and the residuals
$e_i = y_i - \hat{\mu}_i$:

```{r}
head(fitted(fit))
head(residuals(fit))
```

As in [Unit F](un_F.html), the coefficient $R^2$ can be obtained in two
different ways: $$
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{var}(e)}{\text{var}(y)} = \text{cor}(x,y)^2.
$$

```{r}
e <- residuals(fit)
1 - my_var(e) / my_var(y)
cor(x, y)^2
```

```{r}
plot(cherry$diameter, cherry$volume,
  pch = 16,
  xlab = "Diameter (cm)", ylab = "Volume (cubic metres)"
)
abline(fit) # Same as abline(a = beta0_hat, b = beta1_hat)
```

Why exactly this line? Among all the lines $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$, the least squares
line is the one with the [smallest sum of squared residuals]{.orange}
$\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2$, as the following video shows.

{{< video video/un_K_least_squares.mp4 title="Least squares: the line and the sum of squared residuals" >}}

## The linear regression model

So far, as in [Unit F](un_F.html), we have only [described]{.blue} the $31$
trees. But these trees are a sample: we are interested in the relationship
between diameter and volume for [all]{.orange} the black cherry trees of the
forest.

The [simple linear regression model]{.orange} assumes that $$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n,
$$ where the errors $\epsilon_1,\dots,\epsilon_n$ are independent, with
distribution $\text{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. The values $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of the diameter are
treated as [fixed]{.blue}, non-random, numbers: only the errors $\epsilon_i$,
and therefore the volumes $Y_i$, are random. As in [Unit I](un_I.html), capital
letters denote random variables. Therefore:

-   $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are [parameters]{.blue}, and $\hat{\beta}_0$ and
    $\hat{\beta}_1$ are their [estimates]{.blue};
-   $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ is the [mean]{.orange} volume of the trees with
    diameter $x$;
-   $\sigma$ measures how much the volumes vary around this mean.

The variance $\sigma^2$ is estimated by $$
s^2 = \frac{1}{n - 2}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2,
$$ where we divide by $n - 2$ because two parameters, $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$,
have been estimated.

```{r}
n <- nrow(cherry)
s <- sqrt(sum(e^2) / (n - 2))
s
sigma(fit) # The same value, computed by R
```

Note that $s$ is [not]{.orange} the standard deviation of the volumes, computed
by `sd(y)`: it measures how much the volumes vary [around the line]{.blue}.

## The standard error of $\hat{\beta}_1$

Under the model, as for $\bar{Y}$ in [Unit I](un_I.html), we have that $$
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1, \qquad \sigma_{\hat{\beta}_1} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}}.
$$ The estimator $\hat{\beta}_1$ is therefore [unbiased]{.blue}, and its
[standard error]{.orange} decreases with $n$. Replacing $\sigma$ with $s$, we
obtain the estimated standard error, denoted by $\text{s.e.}(\hat{\beta}_1)$ in
the theory lectures:

```{r}
se_hat <- s / sqrt(sum((x - mean(x))^2)) # Estimated standard error
se_hat
```

As for the mean in [Unit J](un_J.html), we have that $$
T = \frac{\hat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{S/\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}} \sim t_{n-2}.
$$ Hence, the tests and the confidence intervals for $\beta_1$ follow the same
recipe of [Unit J](un_J.html), with $n - 2$ degrees of freedom instead of
$n - 1$.

## A test for the slope

Is the diameter related to the volume? If $\beta_1 = 0$, the mean volume does
not depend on the diameter. We test $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ against
$H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0$. Under $H_0$, the test statistic $$
t = \frac{\hat{\beta}_1 - 0}{s/\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}}
$$ has a $t$ distribution with $n - 2$ degrees of freedom.

```{r}
t_obs <- (beta1_hat - 0) / se_hat # Observed test statistic
t_obs
qt(0.975, df = n - 2) # Critical value, significance level 5%
2 * (1 - pt(abs(t_obs), df = n - 2)) # Two-sided P-value
```

The observed statistic falls in the [critical region]{.blue}, $|t| > 2.05$, and
the P-value is practically zero: we [reject]{.orange} $H_0$. Not a surprise,
looking at the scatterplot.

## The command `summary`

All these quantities are reported by the command `summary`:

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

In the table `Coefficients`, for each parameter:

-   `Estimate` is the estimate, $\hat{\beta}_0$ or $\hat{\beta}_1$;
-   `Std. Error` is its estimated standard error;
-   `t value` is the test statistic for $H_0: \beta_0 = 0$ or $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$;
-   `Pr(>|t|)` is the two-sided P-value.

Moreover, `Residual standard error` is $s$, with its $n - 2 = 29$ degrees of
freedom, and `Multiple R-squared` is $R^2$. The last line will be discussed
later in this unit.

## A confidence interval for the slope

As in [Unit J](un_J.html), a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\beta_1$ is $$
\left(\hat{\beta}_1 - t_{0.975,\,n-2} \frac{s}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}}, \ \hat{\beta}_1 + t_{0.975,\,n-2} \frac{s}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}}\right).
$$

```{r}
t_quant <- qt(0.975, df = n - 2) # Quantile of order 0.975
c(beta1_hat - t_quant * se_hat, beta1_hat + t_quant * se_hat)
confint(fit) # Both beta_0 and beta_1, 95% by default
```

With $95\%$ confidence, each additional centimetre of diameter corresponds to
between $0.051$ and $0.062$ m$^3$ of additional timber, on average.

## Prediction

A forester measures a standing tree with a diameter of $40$ cm. As in
[Unit F](un_F.html), the predicted volume is $\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot 40$.
The command `predict` gives the same value, and requires a data frame with
the new values of the explanatory variable:

```{r}
beta0_hat + beta1_hat * 40
new_tree <- data.frame(diameter = 40)
predict(fit, newdata = new_tree)
```

How precise is this prediction? There are [two different questions]{.orange}:

-   what is the [mean volume]{.blue} of all the trees with diameter $40$ cm?
    This is the parameter $\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 40$, and we need a
    [confidence interval]{.blue};
-   what is the volume of [this particular tree]{.blue}? This is a random
    variable, and we need a [prediction interval]{.blue}.

```{r}
predict(fit, newdata = new_tree, interval = "confidence")
predict(fit, newdata = new_tree, interval = "prediction")
```

The prediction interval is much [wider]{.orange}: besides the uncertainty
about $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$, it also accounts for the variability $\sigma$ of the
single trees around the mean.

## Residual plots

The normal linear model relies on four [assumptions]{.orange}, summarised in
the theory lectures by the acronym L.I.N.E.: [L]{.blue}inearity,
[I]{.blue}ndependence, [N]{.blue}ormality and [E]{.blue}qual variance of the
errors. Independence depends on how the data were collected; the other three are
checked through the residuals. First, we plot the residuals $e_i$ against the
fitted values $\hat{\mu}_i$:

```{r}
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit),
  pch = 16,
  xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = "dashed") # Horizontal line at zero
```

If the model were adequate, we would see a [cloud without patterns]{.blue}
around zero. Here, instead, the residuals are positive at the two extremes and
negative in the middle: the relationship is [curved]{.orange}.

A [fan-shaped]{.blue} cloud, with residuals more and more spread out as the
fitted values increase, would instead indicate that the variance is not
constant.

## Diagnostic plots

The tests and the intervals also assume [normal]{.blue} errors; this matters
especially for the prediction intervals. The command
`plot`, applied to the output of `lm`, draws several [diagnostic plots]{.orange}.
We consider the first two:

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) # Two plots side by side
plot(fit, which = 1:2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

-   `Residuals vs Fitted` is the plot of the previous section. The red line
    follows the average trend of the residuals: it should be roughly flat
    around zero, while here it is U-shaped. **R** also labels the three
    observations with the largest residuals: number $31$ is the largest tree.
-   `Q-Q Residuals` (normal Q-Q plot) compares the ordered [standardised
    residuals]{.blue}, that is the residuals divided by their estimated
    standard deviation, with the quantiles of a standard normal distribution.
    If the errors are normal, the points lie close to the dotted line. Here
    they do, apart from small departures at the two extremes: the normality
    assumption is reasonable.

## Extrapolation

Besides the curvature, there is a second problem. For a small tree, the predicted volume is
[negative]{.orange}:

```{r}
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(diameter = 15))
```

The smallest tree in the data has a diameter of $21.1$ cm: predicting outside
the range of the observed data ([extrapolation]{.blue}) is dangerous.

## Adding the height

The volume of a tree does not depend on its diameter only: taller trees have,
on average, more timber.

::: callout-note
#### Research question

Does the [height]{.orange} of a tree help to predict its volume, once the
diameter is known?
:::

## Scatterplot matrix

With three variables, the command `pairs` draws all the scatterplots at once,
and `cor` applied to the data frame returns all the correlations:

```{r}
pairs(cherry, pch = 16)
round(cor(cherry), 2)
```

The volume is strongly related to the diameter and, less strongly, to the
height. Note also that the two explanatory variables are [related to each
other]{.orange}: taller trees tend to have a larger diameter.

## The multiple linear regression model

The [multiple linear regression model]{.orange} with two explanatory variables
assumes that $$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \epsilon_i, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n,
$$ where $x_{i1}$ is the diameter and $x_{i2}$ the height of the $i$th tree.
As in the simple model, the values $x_{i1}$ and $x_{i2}$ are treated as
fixed, and the errors $\epsilon_1,\dots,\epsilon_n$ are independent, with
distribution $\text{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. Therefore:

-   $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2$ is the [mean]{.blue} volume of the
    trees with diameter $x_1$ and height $x_2$;
-   $\beta_1$ is the change in the mean volume when the diameter increases by
    $1$ cm, [at fixed height]{.orange};
-   $\beta_2$ is the change in the mean volume when the height increases by
    $1$ m, [at fixed diameter]{.orange}.

The estimates $\hat{\beta}_0$, $\hat{\beta}_1$ and $\hat{\beta}_2$ are again
obtained by [least squares]{.blue}, that is by minimising $$
\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_{i1} - \beta_2 x_{i2})^2.
$$ There is no simple formula as in [Unit F](un_F.html): we let **R** do the
computations.

## Fitting the model with two variables

The explanatory variables are listed in the formula, separated by `+`:

```{r}
fit2 <- lm(volume ~ diameter + height, data = cherry)
coef(fit2)
```

For two trees with the [same height]{.blue}, one additional centimetre of
diameter corresponds, on average, to $0.053$ m$^3$ of additional timber. For
two trees with the [same diameter]{.blue}, one additional metre of height
corresponds, on average, to $0.031$ m$^3$ of additional timber. In short, we
say that these are the effects of the diameter and of the height, each
[adjusting for]{.orange} the other variable.

## The output of `summary`

```{r}
summary(fit2)
```

The output is read as for the simple model, with a few differences:

-   in the table `Coefficients`, the rows `diameter` and `height` test
    $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ and $H_0: \beta_2 = 0$, that is, whether each variable
    is useful [given the other one]{.blue}. The test statistics are computed as
    for the simple model, estimate divided by standard error, but now have a
    $t$ distribution with $n - 3$ degrees of freedom. The height has a P-value
    of $0.016$: it helps to predict the volume, even when the diameter is
    known;
-   the variance $\sigma^2$ is estimated by $s^2 = \frac{1}{n - 3}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2$,
    because three parameters have been estimated: `Residual standard error` is
    $s$, with $n - 3 = 28$ degrees of freedom;
-   the last line is the [F test]{.orange} of $H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 0$,
    that is, whether [at least one]{.blue} of the variables is useful. Here the
    P-value is practically zero.

The coefficient $R^2$ increases from $0.935$ (diameter only) to $0.948$. It is still defined as
$R^2 = 1 - \text{var}(e)/\text{var}(y)$, but it is no longer the square of the
correlation between $y$ and a single explanatory variable.

## Confidence intervals

As for the simple model, the $95\%$ confidence intervals are obtained with
`confint`:

```{r}
confint(fit2)
```

## Prediction with two variables

Two standing trees have the same diameter, $40$ cm, but different heights,
$20$ m and $25$ m. The data frame given to `predict` must now contain both
variables:

```{r}
new_trees <- data.frame(diameter = c(40, 40), height = c(20, 25))
predict(fit2, newdata = new_trees, interval = "prediction")
```

The taller tree is expected to have about $0.16$ m$^3$ of additional timber.
As before, `interval = "confidence"` would instead give the
intervals for the mean volume.

## Diagnostic plots, again

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit2, which = 1:2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The residuals show the same [curvature]{.orange} seen in the simple model:
adding the height improves the predictions, but it does not fix this problem.
The normal Q-Q plot, instead, does not show strong departures from normality.
The model is useful, but it is only an approximation.
